# Clinical Vignette: Miguel

Miguel was twenty-two when he left San Salvador to visit his grandmother for what he thought would be a two-week holiday. The neighborhood where she lived had grown increasingly unstable over the previous year, but his mother had assured him it would be fine—he would stay indoors mostly, help with repairs to the house, spend time with family. On the fourth day, while walking to a corner store three blocks away, gunfire erupted without warning. Miguel heard the first shots as cracks in the air, then realized they were close—very close. A car nearby had its window shattered. People scattered. Miguel ran toward a narrow alley, his heart hammering so violently he thought it might burst through his ribs. He crouched behind a dumpster for what felt like hours but was probably fifteen minutes, listening to voices shouting, more gunfire, sirens. When silence finally came, he waited another twenty minutes before moving. He made it back to his grandmother's house, locked himself in a bedroom, and did not leave for two days.

That was eighteen months ago. Miguel returned to the United States a week later, telling himself the incident was over, that he was safe now, that he would move forward. But his body had other ideas.

Within weeks of his return, Miguel noticed his muscles never fully relaxed. His shoulders lived near his ears. His jaw clenched so tightly at night that his teeth ached. At his job as a product manager at a mid-sized tech firm, he found himself unable to focus on meetings. His eyes kept drifting to the windows, tracking movement in the parking lot below. When colleagues approached his desk unexpectedly—even his manager, even friends—his entire nervous system would jolt as if the danger were immediate and real. A coworker once wheeled her chair quickly around a corner into his line of sight, and Miguel flinched so violently he knocked his coffee across his keyboard. The humiliation burned, but worse was the certainty that had seized him in that split second: that something terrible was about to happen.

He began checking his body obsessively. In the bathroom at work, he would lift his shirt and scan his torso for marks, for wounds, for any sign that he had been injured and simply hadn't noticed yet. At home, he would run his hands over his arms and legs, feeling for something wrong, something that might prove his body was damaged. The checking never brought relief—it only sharpened his awareness of every sensation, every ache, every irregularity. A small bruise became proof of danger. A muscle twitch became a harbinger.

When the checking failed to settle his mind, Miguel would reach out to friends or his mother, asking them to tell him he was okay, that nothing was wrong with him, that he was safe. He knew, on some level, that the reassurance never lasted—that he would need it again within hours—but in the moment of asking, there was a desperate hope that someone else's certainty could anchor him. His best friend stopped answering his calls as frequently. His mother grew tired of the repetition. He had come to believe that if he was truly in danger, no amount of reassurance would matter anyway, but that if he wasn't, then surely someone could convince him of that fact with enough conviction.

The self-harm began on a night when the tension in his body felt unbearable, when his hypervigilance had been running for sixteen hours straight and his mind was screaming. He pressed a lit cigarette against the inside of his forearm. The sharp, localized pain cut through the noise in his head like nothing else could. For perhaps ten minutes, his body felt like it belonged to him again. The relief was so profound that he did it again the following week, and then again. Now, when the tension becomes intolerable and reassurance has failed, he finds himself in the bathroom with a lighter or a sharp edge, seeking that momentary clarity.

His work performance has begun to suffer. He missed a major product launch meeting last month because he couldn't manage the drive to the office—the highway felt too exposed, too unpredictable. His manager has noticed his distraction, his sudden flinches, his tendency to step away from his desk. Miguel is afraid he will lose this job, and more than that, he is afraid that the fear itself will never leave. What brought him to seek help now was a moment last week when his hands were shaking so badly he couldn't type, and he realized he couldn't remember what it felt like to not be afraid. He wants to know if it is possible to feel safe again, or if the alley in San Salvador has become permanent—if he will spend the rest of his life waiting for the next shot.
